Qatada, whose view is repeated by al-Mawardi, al-Zamakhshari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir, names the Jews and Christians, who claimed their scripture and prophet came first and that they were closer to God. Ibn Zayd says the verse forbade the Prophet from such argument, and al-Qurtubi notes that some understood it as referring to the Quraysh. On the phrase 'after it was answered', most take it as people embracing Islam, while al-Razi, Ibn 'Ashur and al-Alusi read it as God answering His messenger through miracles or victory at Badr, and Ibn 'Atiyya leaves open whether the pronoun refers to God, the religion or the Prophet. The word 'daḥiḍa' is explained as false or slipping. Al-Baghawi and al-Nasafi take the wrath to mean disbelief and the punishment to be in the hereafter. Ibn Kathir reads these words as a warning, and Ibn 'Uthaymin observes that divine wrath is an attribute fitting God's majesty and not comparable to human anger.

The commentators explain that God sent down the Book with truth, meaning in all justice and soundness, and the balance, which stands for justice by which rights are weighed between people. The Prophet is then told that he does not know when the Hour will come, and that it is near. On the general meaning the commentators largely agree: al-Tabari, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Kathir report from Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada that the balance means justice, and Ibn Kathir links this reading to other verses. Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Sam'ani explain that justice is called a balance because the scale is the instrument of fairness among people. In one report Mujahid understands the balance as the familiar weighing instrument, a view that al-Tabari, al-Qurtubi and al-Shinqiti retain while holding that justice includes it. Ibn Juzayy and al-Biqa'i connect the passage to the mention of the Hour, since the Day of Judgment is when deeds are weighed. Most explain the masculine form of 'near' by the fact that the Hour is a time, while al-Kisa'i holds the word serves both genders. In the next verse, the commentators explain that unbelievers ask mockingly for the Hour to come, while believers fear it while knowing it is true, and that those who dispute it are in far-reaching error, since resurrection is not beyond God's power.

The commentators explain that this verse describes two groups facing the Hour. Those who do not believe seek to hasten it, mocking and considering it unlikely, while believers fear it because they know it is true beyond doubt. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Nasafi report that some polytheists asked the Prophet when the Hour would come, in defiance, and that the verse was revealed in that context, according to Ibn Abbas and Muqatil.

Most exegetes agree that the word ishfaq means fear mixed with concern, and that believers dread the Hour because they do not know what awaits them. Al-Baghawi and al-Sam'ani stress that the unbelievers' haste expresses denial. Al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari argue that those who dispute about the Hour are in doubt, and that denying the Resurrection is unreasonable since God created humanity at first and justice demands recompense. Al-Qurtubi and al-Nasafi explain that mira means insistent argument, drawing on the image of milking a camel.

Ibn Kathir cites the well-known hadith of the man who asked the Prophet when the Hour would come and was told to prepare by loving God and His Messenger, since a person is with whom he loves. Ibn Ashur notes that dread of the Hour itself conveys the magnitude of its terrors. The scholars differ mainly in the nuances of their terms rather than in the core meaning of the verse.

This verse states that God is Subtle and Gentle toward His servants, meaning kind and gracious to them, that He gives provision to whom He wills, widening or restricting it according to His wisdom, and that He is the Strong, the Mighty, whom nothing can overcome or resist. The commentators broadly agree on the general meaning. Ibn Abbas explains 'Latif' as 'Attentive to them' and Ikrima as 'Benevolent', while Sudiyy understands it as gentleness. Muqatil holds that God is kind to both the righteous and the sinner, since He does not destroy them by hunger because of their sins; Ibn Kathir, al-Mahalli and al-Suyuti follow this general reading. Qurtubi gathers many definitions, including that of Junayd, that God is gentle toward His friends so that they come to know Him. Al-Baghawi and Abu Hayyan hold that the favours a disbeliever enjoys are not true kindness but a respite and a test, and that true kindness is only what leads to mercy. Al-Razi, Ibn Juzayy and Ibn Ashur distinguish general sustenance, given to all creatures, from the additional abundance that God reserves for whom He wills. Jafar al-Sadiq sees the kindness in provision as lying in God giving lawful goods and not granting them all at once. The following verse, on tilling for the hereafter and for this world, is explained by Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Mawardi: whoever seeks the hereafter has his reward multiplied, and whoever seeks only this world receives a share of it and has no portion in the hereafter. Ibn Kathir relies on a report from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, while Razi and Qurtubi note that this passage is not to be regarded as abrogated.

This verse states that God multiplies the reward of those who work for the Hereafter, while He gives those who work only for this world a portion of worldly provision that He has decreed for them, with no share in the next life. Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn Abbas, Qatada and Mujahid take the word harth (tilling) to mean deeds and gain: whoever seeks the Hereafter has his good deeds increased, and whoever seeks this world receives what was measured out for him. Ibn Kathir links this to a passage in Surat al-Isra, which says God grants the immediate to whom He wills, and he suggests that such a person may lose both worlds if God so decides. Mawardi, Nasafi and Ibn al-Jawzi understand the increase as divine help and facilitation in acts of worship, while Zamakhshari holds that worldly sustenance is an assigned provision that surely reaches its owner. Qurtubi, Nasafi and Abu Hayyan explain that the verse mainly concerns the disbeliever or the one who denies the afterlife, whereas Tabari reads it as applying to anyone who works only for this world. Razi notes that mentioning the Hereafter first signals its superiority and that the image of tilling is a metaphor. Ibn al-Jawzi and Razi cite a hadith from Ubayy ibn Ka'b warning against this attitude. Qurtubi argues the verse is not abrogated because it is a statement of fact, while Muqatil considers it abrogated by the verse in Surat al-Isra.

The commentators explain that this verse rebukes the idolaters for taking partners who have instituted for them in religion what God never permitted. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi understand the partners either as the devils who adorned polytheism, denial of the resurrection and the pursuit of worldly gain alone, or as the idols they made partners of God, to whom the legislation is attributed because they were the cause of the people's misguidance. Most of them take the 'decisive word' to be God's prior decree to delay the punishment until the Last Day; had it not been for this, judgment would have been carried out in this world. The wrongdoers will nonetheless suffer a painful punishment in the next life. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi observe that reading 'wa-anna' with a fatha links it to 'the decisive word', while the common reading with a kasra starts a new sentence. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi specify that the instituted laws include beliefs and customs such as the bahira, the sa'iba, the wasila and the ham. Ibn 'Ashur and Ibn 'Uthaymin add that the verse condemns religious innovation, not the practical arrangements of life that people regulate on sound general principles. All agree that in matters of religion only what God has permitted has authority, and that the punishment of the wrongdoers is reserved for the Hereafter.

This verse describes the scene of the Day of Resurrection: the wrongdoers, meaning the disbelievers and idolaters, will be seen fearful of what they have earned, and the punishment they dread will certainly befall them, as al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Samani explain. By contrast, the believers who did righteous deeds will be in the finest gardens of Paradise, where they will have whatever they wish with their Lord, and this is the great bounty. The commentators agree on this plain meaning, that a rawda is a pleasant, lush place, and that the phrase 'with their Lord' expresses honour and special favour. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and al-Qurtubi see the passage as heightening the terror of punishment and the greatness of reward, while Ibn 'Ashur notes that the fear described is nearly despair, since the punishment is already falling. The following verses about love for the near kin have drawn differing views. Ibn 'Abbas, in the report found in al-Bukhari, takes it as the kinship between the Prophet and the Quraysh, a view shared by Mujahid, Qatada and Ikrima. Sa'id ibn Jubayr and 'Ali ibn al-Husayn understand it as the Prophet's family, while al-Hasan and Qatada read it as drawing closer to God through good deeds. Al-Dahhak held that the verse was abrogated, whereas Ibn Kathir and al-Alusi reject abrogation and prefer the first reading. The commentators present these interpretations without a definitive ruling between them.

The commentators explain that this verse refers to the delights of Paradise, the glad tidings God gives to His believing and righteous servants. God then instructs His Prophet to tell his people that he asks no wage for conveying the message, except that they show affection for him because of the kinship between them. Most exegetes agree that the meaning is to keep the ties of kinship, to protect the Prophet and to spare him harm; Ibn 'Abbas reports that Quraysh were all related to him through some branch, so he asked them to maintain these ties. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn al-Jawzi consider this the strongest reading, with the exception being disconnected, since affection is not really a payment. Al-Hasan al-Basri and Qatada take it to mean drawing near to God through obedience and good deeds. Sa'id ibn Jubayr, 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb, 'Ali ibn al-Husayn and al-Suddi understand it as the Prophet's close kin and family, a view Ibn Kathir discusses, noting that the surah is Meccan. Al-Dahhak and al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl hold that the verse was abrogated, a view many reject. Finally, the verse states that whoever performs a good deed has its reward increased, and that God is forgiving and grateful.

The commentators explain that this verse answers the claim of the Meccan unbelievers that the Prophet had invented the Qur'an against God. Al-Tabari, Qatada and others take the conditional to mean that if God willed, He could seal the Prophet's heart and make him forget the Qur'an, whereas Mujahid and Muqatil understand it as strengthening his heart with patience against their insults. All agree that God's erasing falsehood and establishing truth is a constant practice, carried out through the Qur'an or through His decree. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi add that God would not support someone who lies against Him. The scholars differ on the grammar: al-Kisa'i proposes an inversion, while most, including al-Zajjaj and al-Zamakhshari, treat the clause "God erases falsehood" as an independent statement rather than a consequence of the condition, the missing waw in the written text being an orthographic matter. Ibn Juzayy and Abu Hayyan follow this reading. The verse closes by affirming that God knows what the hearts conceal.

This verse states that God accepts the repentance of His servants when they turn back from their sins toward His oneness and obedience, pardons their evil deeds, and knows everything they do, good or bad, and will reward them for it. The commentators agree that repentance means abandoning sin, regretting it, and resolving not to return to it, and that God accepts it through His mercy. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi describe this acceptance as a great divine favour and cite the hadith about God's joy at the repentance of His servant. Ibn Kathir reports that Ibn Mas'ud, asked about a man who had committed adultery with a woman and then married her, recited this verse. Ali, cited by al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi, lists six elements of true repentance, including remorse, making up neglected duties and returning wrongfully taken property. Opinions differ on whether major sins are forgiven without repentance: Ahl al-Sunna hold that this depends on God's will, while the Mu'tazilites hold that repentance is required, as Ibn Juzayy and Abu Hayyan note. The readers Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Hafs and Khalaf read the verb in the second person, the rest in the third; Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim prefer the third person, since the clause sits between two third-person statements. As for the verb yastajibu, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy take it to mean that God answers the prayers of believers, while others understand the believers as responding to their Lord.

This verse says that God responds to those who believe and do righteous deeds and increases them from His bounty, while the disbelievers will face a severe punishment. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi explain that “yastajib” means to respond, that is, to answer their supplications and give them what they ask, with the extra bounty being that He gives them more than they asked. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir also report, through Qatada and al-Nakha‘i, that this bounty means the believers intercede for their brothers, and those brothers intercede for the brothers of their brothers, a view also attributed to Ibn ‘Abbas. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn ‘Atiyya and al-Razi offer another reading in which the subject of “yastajib” is the believers themselves, who answer their Lord’s call and obey Him, al-Zamakhshari citing Sa‘id ibn Jubayr. Ibn ‘Atiyya and al-Razi take the extra bounty to mean multiplying good deeds, and al-Razi reports a tradition that it means the acceptance of intercession and God’s good pleasure. Abu Hayyan and al-Nasafi favour the meaning of answering, and Ibn Sa‘di explains that God calls His servants to repentance: the one who responds is thanked and rewarded, while the one who refuses faces punishment. The commentators agree that the verse calls to faith and good works, promises the believers a response and an increase, and warns the disbelievers.

This verse explains that if God expanded provision for all His servants, many of them would transgress and some would oppress others, so He sends down their sustenance in a measure of His own choosing, for He is aware of His servants and sees them. The commentators report that it was revealed concerning some of the people of the Suffa who wished for abundance; Khabbab ibn al-Aratt says it was revealed about them because they had coveted the wealth of the Banu Qurayza, the Banu al-Nadir and the Banu Qaynuqa, while 'Amr ibn Huraith and others say it concerns the people of the Suffa. On the meaning of 'baghy', all agree it means transgression and injustice, though they differ on its form. Ibn Abbas explains it as seeking one rank after another and one mount after another, while others see it as craving always for more. Al-Zamakhshari notes that wealth makes one arrogant and insolent and that poverty rarely causes transgression, whereas al-Razi takes the verse as proof that wealth produces tyranny. Al-Tabari and al-Qurtubi note that 'rizq' may here mean rain. Ibn 'Ashur holds that a rich person with a sound soul does not necessarily fall into transgression, and that the verse states a general wisdom in the order of the world. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi also cite the hadith that some servants are reformed only by wealth and others only by poverty.

This verse states that God is the one who sends down the rain that brings relief, after people have despaired of it, and who spreads His mercy. He is the Protector who cares for His servants and the One worthy of praise. The commentators cite the report of ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, who was told that the land was barren and people had despaired, and replied: then you will be given rain. They agree that qunut means despair, and that ghayth is beneficial rain, and that the walī is the one who cares for his servants through his favour. They differ over the mercy mentioned. Muqatil, Mujahid, al-Sudi and Ibn Kathir take it to be the rain itself, while Ibn ʿAtiyya, al-Zamakhshari, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi extend it to its effects such as fertility and growth, and al-Mahdawi takes it to be the sunshine after rain. In the following verses the commentators discuss the creation of the heavens and earth and the creatures scattered within them, and God's power to gather all beings on the Day of Resurrection. Several draw from the verse that the calamities people suffer are due to their own sins, though God forgives much of them. Opinions differ here: some take worldly afflictions as punishment for past sins, while al-Razi and Ibn Juzayy hold that they may be a trial, especially for prophets and the righteous.

The commentators explain that this verse is among the signs of God that show His power and greatness: the creation of the heavens and the earth, the living creatures He has scattered in them, and His ability to gather all creatures after death whenever He wills. They differ on the meaning of 'dabba' (a moving creature). Mujahid includes humans and angels, while al-Farra' and Abu 'Ali al-Farisi take it to refer only to what is on the earth, comparing the verse about pearls and coral coming from 'both seas' though they come only from the salt water. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya follow this reading but find it hard to accept that angels are called dabba. Al-Razi and al-Nasafi allow that angels may move while flying, or that God created walking creatures in the heavens. Ibn Kathir includes angels, jinn, humans and all animals. The pronoun in 'their gathering' is taken by many to refer to rational beings by preponderance, and the gathering is the assembly for judgment on the Last Day. The following verses, on rain after despair and on afflictions caused by what hands have earned, are often read together with this one. Many say that every hardship in the believer's life expiates his sins and that what God pardons in this world will not return in the next, relying on a hadith of Ali ibn Abi Talib, while al-Hasan links the affliction to legal punishments. Others reject that every calamity is a punishment, since this world is a place of trial rather than of recompense. Modern writers such as Sayyid Qutb, Ibn 'Uthaymin and al-Sha'rawi stress the wonders of creation and the still unknown reality of life.

The commentators explain that the misfortunes which befall people in their persons, their possessions and their families come about because of what their own hands have earned, meaning their sins, and that God pardons many of them. Ibn Abbas, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi report that these trials can serve as expiation in this world, so that the punishment is not repeated in the next, and they cite hadiths saying that whatever afflicts a believer, even a thorn or a scratch, is due to a sin, and that God pardons more than that. Ali, quoted by Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, considered this the most hopeful verse in the Quran. Al-Hasan al-Basri takes the misfortune here to mean the legal penalties (hudud) imposed for sins. Al-Zamakhshari holds that the verse concerns criminals, while those who have committed no crime, such as prophets and children, receive such afflictions as compensation and for their benefit. Al-Razi reports that some denied that worldly calamities are punishments, citing the verse saying that today every soul will be recompensed for what it earned, and the fact that the righteous are often tested more severely, since this world is a place of trial. Those who hold the general sense answer that these afflictions may be a test or a raising of rank. Ibn al-Qayyim sees in the verse both good news and a warning, and Ibn Kathir transmits these reports without deciding between them. The readers differ on the particle fa in the phrase fa-bima kasabat: Nafi and Ibn Amir omit it, while the majority read it, a difference that scarcely alters the meaning.

The commentators explain that the verse addresses people, and some restrict it to the polytheists: no one can escape God's power when He wills to punish them, and no one besides Him can be a protector who shields them from His punishment or a helper who defends them. The verse follows the statement that God forgives many sins although He could punish them, so this forgiveness is a grace and not a sign of weakness. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir understand worldly afflictions as consequences of sins, citing hadiths transmitted from the Prophet, from 'Ali and from 'Imran ibn Husayn. Al-Hasan al-Basri takes the affliction to mean the legal punishments imposed for transgressions. Al-Razi argues that not every pain is a punishment, since this world is a place of trial rather than of recompense, and that prophets and righteous people are tested more often. Al-Zamakhshari limits the verse to criminals, whereas al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir apply it to both believers and disbelievers. The readers differ on the particle fa in the phrase "fa-bima": Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read it without fa, while the others read it with fa. The general meaning remains that a person cannot flee God's decree, and that the true refuge is God alone.

The commentators explain that this verse cites among God's signs the ships that sail the sea: al-Jawari means the ships and al-a'lam means the mountains, since large vessels appear on the water as tall as mountains. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and most early exegetes understand that, if God wills, He stills the wind and the ships stand motionless on the surface of the water, neither advancing nor retreating; Qatada, Ibn 'Abbas and al-Sudi are cited in this sense. All agree that the passage is a lesson for everyone who is patient in hardship and thankful in ease, which al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi connect with the two qualities of the believer. Al-Razi adds that the verse proves the existence of a powerful and wise Creator and recalls the benefits of sea transport and trade. Several scholars, including al-Mawardi, Ibn Kathir and al-Nasafi, add that God could also destroy the ships with a violent wind because of the sins of their passengers, while pardoning many faults; Ibn 'Ashur sees here a reminder of divine power in both situations. The recitations differ on 'ya'fu' (jussive, indicative or subjunctive) and on 'ya'lama'; Abu Hayyan and al-Zamakhshari examine these variants. For most exegetes, the end of the verse warns those who dispute God's signs: at the moment of drowning or after the resurrection they will understand that they have no refuge from Him.

This verse describes ships sailing the sea, as large as mountains, as one of God's signs. If He wills, He stills the wind and the ships stand motionless on the water; if He wills, He sends a violent wind that sinks them because of the sins of those aboard, while pardoning much. This verse belongs to a passage listing God's signs: ships gliding across the sea like mountains. God states that if He willed, He could still the wind so the vessels stand motionless on the water, or drown them because of the sins of those aboard, while pardoning many of those sins. The commentators agree on the basic meaning: drowning is the consequence of sin, and God forgives much. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Nasafi explain that 'al-jawari' means the ships and that 'yubiqhunna' means destroying them by drowning. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi take the verb as applying to the ships themselves, while Ibn Juzayy and al-Tabari take 'kasabu' to refer to the passengers. On grammar, opinions differ: al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Nasafi attach 'aw yubiqhunna' to 'yuskin al-rih', while others treat it separately. On the reading of 'wa ya'lam', Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read it in the nominative, the others in the accusative, and al-Tabari considers both correct. Al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan explain the accusative as the so-called 'waw al-sarf', or as implying an understood 'an'. For 'ma lahum min mahis', al-Tabari and al-Sudi understand it as having no refuge, while Qutrub understands it as having no escape. Several commentators, including Ibn Kathir, al-Tha'alibi and Ibn 'Ashur, connect the passage to the principle that every hardship results from a sin, and to God's abundant pardon. Al-Wahidi regarded it as the most hopeful verse in the Quran.

This verse continues the signs of God at sea: if He wills, He stills the wind so the ships stand motionless on the water, or He drowns them for the sins of their people, while pardoning much. It then says that those who dispute God's signs will know that they have no escape. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan explain that 'mahis' means a way of escape or a refuge, a meaning also given by al-Suddi and Qutrub. Ibn al-Jawzi, citing Ibn Qutayba, takes 'yubiqhunna' to mean drowning them. On recitation, Nafi' and Ibn Amir read 'wa ya'lamu' in the nominative as a new sentence, while the others read it in the subjunctive. Al-Zamakhshari links the subjunctive to an implied purpose, 'so that He may punish them and know', while Sibawayh and al-Zajjaj propose an implied 'an' after the waw. Al-Zamakhshari finds the latter weak for so widely transmitted a reading. Ibn 'Ashur sees the nominative as a threat to the polytheists and the subjunctive as a warning of imminent punishment. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi draw from the verse a call to monotheism and to recognising God's power.

This verse establishes that whatever a person is given in this world, whether wealth, children or standing, is only a passing enjoyment that is used during life and then ends, while what is with God, the reward and bliss of the hereafter, is better in itself and more lasting, and it is for those who believe and put their trust in their Lord. The commentators agree on this basic meaning: al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi stress that worldly life is perishable and what is with God endures, and Ibn Kathir sees in it a way of belittling the world and preferring the lasting to the fleeting. Al-Sa'di adds that the bliss of the hereafter is free of any troubles. Ibn 'Ashur explains that the address may be to the polytheists, while its general sense includes the believers, and that the first fa links the verse to what precedes it, namely the safety of the ships. Almost all agree that the quality joined to faith here is trust in God, understood as relying on Him to bring benefit and avert harm. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Qurtubi and al-Nasafi report that the verse was revealed about Abu Bakr, who gave away all his wealth and was blamed by people, but other works do not repeat this occasion of revelation. Ibn Juzayy lists the virtues of the perfect believers that follow, and Ibn 'Atiyya considers prayer, consultation, spending and measured retaliation to belong to this description. Al-Razi notes that the word 'mata' signals the small worth of the present life. The commentators present these views without deciding between them.

The commentators explain that this verse describes a quality of the believers who avoid major sins and grave immoralities, and who, when angered, forgive and refrain from retaliating. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report that the "major sins" are those for which the law threatens punishment, while the "immoralities" are gross sins that carry a legal penalty, such as fornication, according to Mujahid and Muqatil. Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn al-Jawzi note that immoralities belong to the major sins but are named separately because of their gravity. The reading of Hamza and al-Kisa'i, "kabira al-ithm" in the singular, is explained by Ibn 'Abbas as meaning associationism, though al-Razi finds this far-fetched since faith is already mentioned.

Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir explain that anger is singled out for forgiveness because it is hard to control, so restraining it reflects a high moral quality. Ibn Zayd reports that these qualities were attributed to the Ansar, while others take them as a general praise. Ibn Kathir cites many examples of the Prophet forgiving rather than avenging himself, except when Allah's limits were violated.

The commentators agree that retaliation against injustice is permitted and that an equal requital is lawful, but that pardon and reconciliation are more meritorious and carry a reward from Allah. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi explain that forgiveness is praiseworthy when it restores peace, while retaliation is not blameworthy when it does not exceed the limit. Opinions differ on abrogation: some consider the verse abrogated by the verse on fighting, while others hold it to be valid and unabrogated. The commentators leave the final judgment on this point to the reader.

This verse describes the believers who deserve what is with God, which is better and lasting. They are those who answered their Lord when He called them to His oneness and obedience, who establish the prayer properly, whose affairs are decided by mutual consultation, and who spend from what We have provided them. Several commentators say the verse was first aimed at the Ansar of Medina, as Ibn Zayd reported, while others read it as a general description of anyone with these qualities. Al-Mawardi and al-Naqqash note that consultation was already the custom of the Ansar before the Prophet came to them, and al-Hasan al-Basri said that no people consult together without being guided to the best of their affairs. On spending, al-Suddi takes it to mean zakat, al-Mawardi also allows spending from lawful earnings, and al-Nasafi speaks of charity in general. On the prayer, Qatada understands it as keeping to its appointed times, while Sa'id ibn Jubayr understands it as performing it with all its conditions. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi add that consultation concerns matters on which no revealed text exists, not the rulings already set by God. The commentators also mention consultation in war, in choosing a caliph, and in giving legal opinions, and the exact scope of the verse is known to God alone.

This verse in Surat al-Shura describes a quality of believers who deserve what is with God: when wrongdoing befalls them, they defend themselves without going beyond what is due. The commentators differ on who the aggressor is. Al-Tabari reports the view that it refers to a polytheist who oppresses a Muslim, but he prefers the broader reading that any wrongdoer whom the victim rightly resists is meant, a view followed by al-Suddi. Ibn Zayd links the verse to the polytheists and considers it abrogated by the verse on fighting, while others hold it to be valid. Ibn Atiyya and al-Qurtubi note that self-defence is permitted, that jurists disagree on whether a private person may take back his right without the authority of a judge, and that pardon is generally more excellent. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi relay al-Nakha'i's explanation: believers disliked being humiliated, and when able, they forgave. Al-Razi seeks to reconcile this with the verses praising forgiveness, distinguishing a pardon that calms conflict from one that emboldens the wrongdoer. Ibn Kathir stresses that the Prophet never took revenge for himself, except when God's sacred limits were violated. Several commentators, including Ibn Kathir and al-Tha'alibi, read the retaliation clause as requiring a response equal to the offence. Views on finer applications, such as insults or debts, remain varied among these scholars, and the commentators cited do not settle them.

This verse states that a person who suffers wrongdoing may defend himself, then specifies that the retribution for an evil is an equal evil, without excess. Whoever pardons and restores harmony with the offender has his reward with God, for God does not love wrongdoers. The commentators agree on the principle of measured reciprocity and on the value of forgiveness, but differ on the verse's scope. Al-Tabari holds that it applies to any aggressor, and mentions Ibn Zayd's view that it concerned polytheists and was abrogated. Al-Shafi'i, Abu Hanifa, Sufyan al-Thawri, Muqatil and Hisham ibn Hujayr limit the rule to retaliation for wounds, while Mujahid and al-Suddi extend it to insults: one answers an abusive word with a similar word, without lying or slander. Ibn Abbas explains that the wrongdoers meant are those who start the aggression. Al-Razi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir stress that pardon is more meritorious than retaliation, and Ibn Kathir cites a hadith in which God increases the honour of one who forgives. Ibn Atiyya reports that Malik forbids a victim to recover property by himself, whereas others permit it. The commentators do not settle these differences, and all the opinions remain presented side by side.

The commentators explain that this verse means that whoever defends himself after being wronged incurs neither blame nor punishment, since he takes back his right without excess, whereas the blame and the sanction fall on those who begin to wrong people and spread corruption on earth without right. Most agree that retaliation is permitted but not obligatory, that forgiveness and reconciliation are preferable, and that the response must stay equal to the offence. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi regard the verse as firm, the retaliation meaning proportionate redress for wounds, and Ibn Kathir cites the report that forgiveness only increases a person's honour. Mujahid and al-Suddi explain that returning evil with evil means answering an insult with a similar insult. The disagreement concerns the scope of the verse: al-Tabari and Ibn Zayd relate it either to Muslims or to polytheists, Ibn Zayd holding it abrogated by the verse of fighting in the latter case, while Muqatil, Abu Hanifa, al-Shafi'i and Sufyan limit the equal return to retaliation for wounds. Al-Razi and Ibn 'Atiyya report that most scholars allow a victim to recover his right himself, whereas Malik forbids it in the case of a breach of trust, al-Shafi'i permitting it. Al-Qurtubi distinguishes retaliation against an unbeliever, which he deems obligatory, from retaliation against a Muslim, which is merely permitted. Ibn 'Ashur sees in it an allusion to defence against aggression, especially at Mecca.

This part of the verse clarifies that accountability and punishment fall only on those who wrong people and act with insolence on earth without right, and that they will suffer a painful punishment. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that wronging means attacking others in their bodies, property or honour, and that transgression on earth means exceeding what God has permitted, committing sins and spreading corruption. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi hold that wronging means initiating harm, and that transgression means arrogance, domination and corruption. Ibn 'Atiyya sees transgression as a form of wrongdoing that the verse singles out to stress its gravity. Al-Mawardi reports that transgression concerns lives and property according to most scholars, while Muqatil understands it as committing sins, and Abu Malik links it to the hope of the Quraysh that a religion other than Islam would remain in Mecca. Abu Hayyan, Ibn Juzayy and al-Qasimi emphasise that the punishment is painful in the hereafter. Al-Qurtubi notes that Ibn Zayd considers the ruling abrogated for polytheists, whereas Qatada takes it as general, and Ibn 'Ashur holds that it covers every wrongdoer, whether polytheist or Muslim. The commentators do not settle these differences.

This part of the verse says that whoever endures harm patiently, without retaliating, and forgives the one who wronged him, has acted according to the firm resolutions that God has enjoined or recommended to His servants, which is a high degree of virtue. The commentators generally understand patience (sabr) as enduring insult and refraining from retaliation, and forgiveness (ghafr) as overlooking the wrong and concealing it. Al-Tabari notes a grammatical ellipsis, so the sentence means that this, on his part, is among the firm resolutions. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir treat forgiveness as recommended, while Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Razi stress that retaliation in kind is permitted and that forgiveness is more meritorious. Al-Qurtubi cites the hadith of the call on the Day of Resurrection for those who pardoned. Al-Kalbi and al-Farra' relate that the verses were revealed concerning Abu Bakr, who was insulted by an Ansari, answered him, then fell silent. Ibn 'Ashur explains that patience and pardon are praiseworthy for believers, and that the scope of forgiveness depends on what the public interest requires. Al-Razi and others observe that such patience requires great strength of character, since the desire for revenge is strong when one has an adversary.

The commentators explain that this verse follows on from what precedes it: whoever God leads astray because of his wrongdoing and rejection of the truth will find, after that misguidance, no ally to guide him or shield him from punishment. When the wrongdoers, meaning for most commentators the polytheists, see the punishment, they ask whether there is any way back. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir understand this as a request to return to the world, and Ibn Kathir links it to other verses where the disbelievers wish to be sent back to act differently. Al-Sudi holds the same view, while Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Alusi also allow the sense of averting the punishment, and al-Qurtubi reports the request to return in order to obey God. On the word 'leads astray', the commentators differ. Al-Zamakhshari, following the Mu'tazili position that God does not create evil, reads it as abandonment, whereas al-Razi, following the Sunni view, takes it as genuine misguidance willed by God. Ibn 'Ashur sees it as God withholding right guidance once a person has sunk deeper into error. On the humiliation of the wrongdoers before the Fire and their furtive glance, Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid explain it as abasement, Qatada and al-Sudi as stealing a glance out of fear, while al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj take it as a look of the heart, since they will be raised blind. All agree that the verse warns the disbelievers and consoles the Prophet ﷺ, and that the believers say the true losers are those who have lost their own souls and their families on the Day of Resurrection.

The verse describes the state of the wrongdoers on the Day of Resurrection: they are brought before the Fire, humbled and abject, glancing at it with stealthy, fearful eyes. Then the believers declare that the true losers are those who lost themselves and their families on the Day of Resurrection, and that the wrongdoers are in a lasting punishment that never ends. The commentators, including al-Tabari, al-Samʿani, al-Baghawi, al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Kathir and al-Jalalayn, agree that the wrongdoers here are the disbelievers and idolaters, and that humility (khushuʿ) means a submission born of abasement and fear, not of reverence. On the phrase 'a furtive glance', opinions differ: Ibn ʿAbbas and Mujahid take it to mean a humiliated glance, Qatada, al-Suddi and Muhammad ibn Kaʿb to mean a glance stolen out of fear of the Fire, while others read it as a glance of the heart, since they will be raised blind, an interpretation some find strained. Al-Mawardi lists three readings of who is presented to the Fire: most idolaters, the people of Pharaoh specifically according to Ibn Masʿud, or idolaters shown their punishment in their graves. Ibn ʿAtiyya and al-Razi note that the believers' words may have been spoken in this world or on the Day of Resurrection, and that the final sentence may be their speech or God's. Al-Alusi attaches the Day of Resurrection to the word 'lost'. Al-Razi and al-Shawkani explain that losing one's family means gaining nothing from them if they are in the Fire, and being separated from them if they are in Paradise, with some adding that it refers to the houris promised to one who had believed.

The commentators explain that this verse states that on the Day of Resurrection the disbelievers will have no allies to protect them from Allah's punishment, and that whomever Allah leads astray has no path, either to guidance in this world or to Paradise in the next. Most agree that guidance and misguidance are in Allah's hand alone. Al-Tabari explains that Allah forsakes whoever He wills from the path of truth, and Ibn Kathir states that whoever Allah misguides has no guide. Al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi report that when the wrongdoers see the punishment they will wish to return to the world.

Most take the 'allies' to be those who would ward off the punishment, while al-Sudi and Mujahid understand 'nakir' as a helper or someone who could change their condition. Al-Tabari links the following verse, which calls people to answer their Lord before a day that cannot be turned back, to this passage.

Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi record other readings of the neighbouring verses. For the 'furtive glance', Mujahid takes it as a humbled look, Qatada and al-Sudi as a stolen glance out of fear, and some say the disbelievers see with the heart because they are raised blind, an opinion transmitted by al-Farra and al-Zajjaj. Al-Razi notes the Qur'an describes the Day of Resurrection in varied terms without deciding between these views.

This verse calls people to answer their Lord before the Day arrives that cannot be turned back, a Day on which they will have no refuge and no means of denial. The commentators agree that it is an urgent call to faith and obedience before it is too late, and a warning against delay. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi explain that the refuge (malja') is a place to shelter in, while Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi take it as a means of salvation. On the word nakir, Mujahid, al-Mawardi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir understand it as a helper who could repel the punishment, whereas al-Zamakhshari, al-Sam'ani, Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Juzayy render it as the act of denying one's deeds, which Ibn 'Atiyya takes as a verbal noun. Al-Qurtubi, Abu Hayyan and Ibn 'Ashur note that it could also be an active participle, though this is considered less likely. Ibn 'Uthaymin reconciles the meaning of denial with the verse of the Cattle, where the disbelievers first deny and then confess when their limbs testify. Al-Biqa'i and Ibn Sa'di add that death ends the possibility of action, so one must hasten without postponing.

This verse tells the Prophet ﷺ that if people turn away, he is not responsible for watching over their deeds; his duty is only to convey the message, as al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Nasafi explain. Most commentators understand 'man' as mankind in general: when God grants a blessing such as wealth or health, people rejoice with arrogance, and when a misfortune such as poverty or illness strikes them because of their sins, they forget the blessings and deny them. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya, however, hold that only the disbelievers are meant, since only they can be rightly struck by what their hands have done. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir apply the verse broadly to all. Al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi take the mercy to mean wealth, health or rain, and the evil to mean famine, sickness or poverty. Al-Mawardi notes that 'kafur' may mean ingratitude for blessings or disbelief in God. Ibn al-Qayyim observes that 'idha' is used for the blessing because it is frequent and certain, and 'in' for the misfortune because it is rare. Ibn 'Ashur sees the verse as consoling the Prophet about a trait found in human nature in general. Ibn 'Uthaymin holds that the duty to convey the message has not been abrogated, against what al-Jalalayn and al-Jawzi mention about abrogation by the verses on fighting.

This verse states that the dominion of the heavens and the earth belongs to God alone, that He creates what He wills, and that He distributes offspring as He pleases: to some He gives only daughters, to some only sons, to some both, and He makes some barren. The commentators agree that the meaning is general and that children are a gift from God that does not depend on human choice. Mujahid, Abu 'Ubayda and al-Dahhak explain that "daughters" means daughters without sons, and "sons" sons without daughters. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report this sense, while most note that "sons and daughters" refers to the joining of both sexes, which Mujahid understood as a child born alternately, boy then girl, and Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyya as twins. The barren one is the person who has no children, according to Ibn 'Abbas.

Commentators noted that daughters are mentioned first even though sons are generally more honoured. Al-Zamakhshari explains that the context presents God as doing what He wills rather than what man wills, and that the Arabs regarded daughters as a burden, so they are placed first to emphasise their importance. Al-Razi and Ibn al-Qayyim also see an intention of kindness and reassurance toward daughters, and Ibn al-Qayyim cites the hadith of Wathila ibn al-Asqa' on the blessing of a first-born daughter. Some, such as al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir, report that the verse was revealed about the prophets: Lot had only daughters, Abraham only sons, Muhammad both, and Yahya and 'Isa were barren. Most scholars, however, hold these as illustrations and treat the rule as general.

The verse ends with "He is All-Knowing, All-Powerful". Al-Tabari understands this as God's knowledge of what He creates and His power to do what He wills, and al-Zamakhshari as His knowledge of what is good for people.

The commentators explain that this verse affirms that God owns the heavens and the earth and creates what He wills: He grants daughters to whom He wills, sons to whom He wills, both sexes together to whom He wills, and renders barren whom He wills, all in accordance with His knowledge and power. Most agree that the word translated as pairing here means combining males and females, and that the gift is granted without return. Reasons for mentioning daughters first differ: al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and others report that the Arabs regarded daughters as a trial, which justifies naming them first, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi stress that the context concerns God's action rather than human desire, and al-Razi offers several further reasons. On how this pairing happens, Mujahid describes a boy then a girl born in alternation, while Ibn al-Hanafiyya speaks of twins, a boy and a girl; al-Qurtubi also cites an interpretation linked to Adam and Eve, attributed to Ibn al-Arabi. Al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir and al-Nasafi mention a report that the verse was first about the prophets: Lot had only daughters, Abraham only sons, Muhammad both, and Yahya and Isa were barren, while holding that its meaning is general. Ibn Kathir and al-Sa'di see four categories of people. Al-Sha'rawi stresses that these gifts signal neither divine approval nor displeasure towards a person, and Ibn 'Uthaymin draws the legal conclusion that a wife may seek annulment if her husband is found barren. The main differences concern the details of how the sexes are combined and which prophets are meant, while there is no real disagreement on the general sense of the verse.

This verse sets out the three ways in which God speaks to humans: a hidden inspiration cast into the heart or given in a dream, speech heard from behind a veil, as Moses heard it, or the sending of an angelic messenger who conveys what God wills. Several commentators report the occasion of revelation: Jews or Quraysh asked the Prophet to speak to God and see Him as Moses did, and the verse answers by describing these modes of communication. Most agree that inspiration, the first mode, is waḥy in the basic sense of a swift hidden communication. The veil is understood by most as hearing without seeing, and the messenger is usually Gabriel. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi hold that speech from behind a veil was granted to Moses and to Muhammad during the Night Journey, while al-Razi and Ibn 'Atiyya think the verse does not settle whether God can be seen. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi understand the veil as a speech God creates in some object, with no possibility of vision. On recitation, Nafi' reads the verbs in the nominative, while the majority read them in the subjunctive, which changes the grammar of the phrase. As for 'a spirit from Our command', Ibn 'Abbas takes it to be the Quran, while others take it to mean prophethood or mercy. All agree that revelation happens only by God's permission and according to His will. The verse thus leads into the presentation of the Quran as a spirit and a light through which God guides whom He wills.

The commentators explain that God tells His Prophet ﷺ that He revealed the Qur'an to him, which He calls a "spirit" because hearts come to life through it as bodies live through the soul, and that it is part of God's command. The verse means that before revelation the Prophet did not know what the Book was or the details of faith and its laws; yet God made the Qur'an a light by which He guides whom He wills among His servants, and the Prophet guides to the straight path, which is Islam, the path of God to whom belongs all that is in the heavens and the earth, and to whom all matters return.

The commentators broadly agree that the "spirit" is the Qur'an or revelation: al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi take it as mercy or revelation, while al-Kalbi and al-Rabi' take it as the Book or Gabriel, and Ibn 'Abbas as prophethood. As for "faith", al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Khuzayma understand it as prayer or the precepts of faith, Abu al-'Aliya as the call to faith, al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Atiyya as the details of the law, while al-Razi and Ibn Juzayy take it as knowledge reachable only by revelation. Al-Mawardi holds that the meaning is that you did not know the Book before the mission.

Opinions differ on whether prophets were believers before their mission: al-Qurtubi and 'Iyad hold that they were preserved from ignorance of God and from associating partners with Him, while al-Zamakhshari argues that the faith denied here is what is known only through revelation. Ibn al-Qayyim draws from this verse that the Qur'an is the life of hearts and their light. Al-Razi and Ibn Kathir describe the modes of revelation: inspiration, speech from behind a veil, and sending an angel. Al-Qurtubi also discusses whether the Prophet followed an earlier law before his mission, a question on which scholars do not settle definitively.

The commentators explain that this verse closes the account of the ways God speaks to His prophets, and that the Qur'an revealed to the Prophet ﷺ is called a "spirit" because hearts come alive through it as bodies do through the soul. Al-Tabari and al-Suddi take "a spirit from Our command" to mean revelation, al-Hasan and Qatada to mean mercy, while al-Kalbi and al-Dahhak identify it as the Book or the Qur'an. As for "you did not know what the Book was, nor faith," al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir read it as meaning that the Prophet did not know the Qur'an or the details of the law before it was revealed; Ibn Khuzayma takes "faith" here to mean prayer, Abu al-'Aliya takes it to mean the call to faith, and Ibn al-Jawzi says it refers to the details of the sacred law. Most commentators refer the pronoun in "We made it a light" to the Qur'an and read "by which We guide whom We will" as guidance, while the Prophet's guiding to a straight path means calling people to it. They agree that the "path of God" is Islam, that God owns whatever is in the heavens and on earth, and that "unto God all affairs return" is both a warning and a promise concerning resurrection and recompense, when God alone judges. Several expand on the three modes of revelation: inspiration, speech from behind a veil as with Moses, and sending an angel, with al-Razi holding that inspiration deserves the name revelation most.
